## @yonasbe - Anthropic's CI playbook: five GitHub Actions optimizations
> Anthropic's CI playbook (give this to your agent)
>
> @AnthropicAI's CI jobs grew 25x in six months, so they built their own test selection system. The same ideas work on GitHub Actions:
>
> 1. Run only affected tests: use the dependency graph from Turborepo, Nx, Bazel, Gradle, Vitest or Jest on PRs.
> 2. Keep the full suite where it counts: run everything on main and in the merge queue.
> 3. Skip workflows a change can't affect: path filters plus job-level ifs so required checks don't hang.
> 4. Run CI once per change: drop the push + pull_request double trigger.
> 5. Bound flaky jobs: set timeout-minutes from the job's run history (default hang is 6 hours).
>
> Anthropic's merges went from about 2,500 a day in May to over 30,000 in September; advice is to "assume your architecture will be at a 25x load within two quarters" 📈

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/yonasbe/status/2112221235333722255
- **Link:** https://starsling.dev/blog/anthropic-ci
- **Filed:** [anthropic-ci-playbook.md](./knowledge/articles/anthropic-ci-playbook.md)
- **What:** Thread distilling Anthropic's CI scaling lessons into five GitHub Actions tactics: affected-test selection, full suite on main/merge queue, path filters, single-trigger runs and job timeouts. Promotes StarSling's longer list of 70+ optimizations.

## @JPoehnelt - Tips for self-hosted GitHub Actions runners (k8s, pnpm store, job pools)
> Some tips for your custom GitHub action runners:
>
> - Preinstall your tooling. I run this via k8s and build off a container image in the repo so each job starts with a matching base.
> - Keep pnpm's persistent store and workspaces on the same filesystem on fast local storage so installs can hardlink packages. Skip GitHub action cache.
> - Separate lightweight checks, heavy builds, and Docker workloads into dedicated pools.
> - Figure out peak loads [...] I oversubscribe the k8s nodes.
> - Consolidate tiny jobs [...] Look at your checkouts.

## @duckdb - DuckDB blog walks an Iceberg table's JSON/Avro/Parquet file tree with plain SQL
> What's Inside an Iceberg Table? 🧊 📦
>
> An Apache Iceberg table looks like a regular table when you query it, but beneath the surface…well, it's like an iceberg. 😅
>
> Underneath, you'll find a small tree of files: one JSON file at the top, a few layers of Avro files in the middle, and Parquet files at the bottom. When something is slow or looks wrong, it helps to know what's in that tree.
>
> DuckDB can read all three formats, so you can inspect every layer with plain SQL. In this post, we create a small Iceberg table, change it a few times, and then walk through the files from the top down.
>
> #ApacheIceberg #DuckDB

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/duckdb/status/2110837648298541271
- **Link:** https://duckdb.org/2026/10/13/inside-iceberg-table?utm_source=x&utm_medium=social
- **Filed:** [duckdb-inside-iceberg-table.md](./knowledge/articles/duckdb-inside-iceberg-table.md)
- **What:** An Iceberg table is a tree of a JSON metadata file, Avro manifest lists and manifests, and Parquet data and delete files. Since DuckDB reads all three formats, each layer can be inspected with SQL to debug slow or wrong tables.

## @kloss_xyz - Seven AGENTS.md rules to keep vibe-coding agents honest
> If you're vibe coding, you need to add these 7 rules to your AGENTS.md:
>
> 1. Never edit, skip, or delete a test to make it pass. Confirm each test would fail if the code did nothing.
> 2. Before adding any dependency, confirm it exists on the official registry, who maintains it, and when it last shipped. Never guess a package name.
> 3. Before using any library's API, check the installed version and read its actual docs or source.
> 4. Never say a task is done until proven against the real thing; show actual output.
> 5. If two fixes fail the same way, stop and question the shared assumption.
> 6. Only change what a task requires; list other issues instead of fixing them.
> 7. Never delete untracked files or data, rewrite git history, or force-push without showing the exact command and waiting for approval.

## @yonasbe - Linear's 15-step GitHub Actions CI speedup playbook (StarSling)
> Linear's CI playbook (for GitHub Actions):
>
> 1. Faster runners: jobs 34% faster, typecheck 52% faster.
> 2. Native type-checking: tsc to tsgo cut typecheck weekly median 73%.
> 3. Lint without types: syntax-only rules, API lint 68% faster, repo 55% faster.
> 4. Oxlint cut runner minutes on linting.
> 5. Lighter checkouts: shallow fetch 94s to 20s; no checkout 27s to 7s.
> 6. Resilient checkout: retry and abort stalled fetch after ~30s.
> 7. Off the critical path: cache write move saved 42s per API PR.
> 8. Preinstall in CI image: Postgres client saved 7-8s per shard.
> 9. Filtered installs: pnpm install 44-73s to 16-18s.
> 10. Drop a costly cache: node_modules cache slower than fresh install.
> 11. Schema snapshots: DB setup ~12s to 1-2s per container.
> 12. Batch short checks: 7 jobs into 2 saved ~87,000 runner-minutes/month.
> 13. Balance shards: 4 to 8 shards, ~19% faster and cheaper.
> 14. Share module state: slowest shard 300-379s to ~195s.
> 15. Setup bounds sharding: 8 shards now use less setup than 4 did.
>
> If you want your CI to look like theirs with all of these optimizations (and 50+ more), give your agent this post:

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/yonasbe/status/2110045850852634825
- **Link:** https://starsling.dev/blog/linear-ci
- **Filed:** [starsling-linear-ci-playbook.md](./knowledge/articles/starsling-linear-ci-playbook.md)
- **What:** StarSling packages Linear's 15 CI optimizations (faster runners, tsgo, Oxlint, shallow checkouts, schema snapshots, shared module state, shard rebalancing) as copy-paste agent prompts mapped to ci-speedup patterns.

## @stretchcloud - Uber's MCP gateway: 800+ servers, 5,000+ tools, and why you probably should not build one
> Most teams building an MCP gateway this quarter are about to relearn what Uber already spent real engineering time on, and most of them don't have what Uber built it on top of. The gateway now fronts over 800 MCP servers and 5,000+ tools, mostly auto-generated.
>
> Control plane (registry) plus data plane (proxy translating MCP to HTTP, gRPC, TChannel). A crawler uses an LLM to write tool descriptions. Every server starts disabled, description changes need owner-approved diffs, ABAC per tool, PII redacted by default.

## @rauchg - gdp-ts: Ghosts of Departed Proofs for TypeScript
> Introducing gdp-ts: Ghosts of Departed Proofs for TypeScript.
>
> gdp-ts is a library, linter and AI skill for safer API design. Under this contract, sensitive functions require 'proofs' that the caller performed an authorization check.
>
> The typechecker verifies these proofs at compile time, preventing your team and agents from shipping catastrophic security (and other kinds of) bugs.
>
> While these patterns have existed for quite some time, especially in ecosystems like Haskell, human code review and cognitive and syntactic overhead made these solutions niche.
>
> The situation is now inverted. Agents are writing more code than we can review, and they *thrive* in tight loops with hard constraints that would frustrate us. We see this with the rise of Rust, borrow checker, code aesthetics debate and all.
>
> The README and examples model a real-world Vercel API product constraint: changing the password on a Project requires a proof of a certain role + a certain entitlement. Thanks to Matt Noonan and Ollie Charles for their research in this space.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/rauchg/status/2107119811444748555
- **Link:** https://github.com/rauchg/gdp-ts
- **What:** Vercel's Guillermo Rauch released a TypeScript library, linter and AI skill using the Ghosts of Departed Proofs pattern so sensitive functions need compile-time proof of an authorization check. Thesis: agents write more code than humans can review, so hard type-level constraints are now worth the overhead.

## @HamelHusain - Review of Anthropic's new Claude eval-building workflow: strong issue discovery, but evals before data
> Put this through its paces yesterday. Some thoughts:
>
> The Bad:
>
> 1. The workflow creates evals before looking at data, and has you correct its mistakes. I believe you should be looking at data first to inform your understanding and to prioritize what to work on before trying to write evals.
> 2. It created markdown files for looking at data and asked us to "tell it" which labels were off. You should create your own annotation app instead. You are using coding agents after all (we did this in our livestream)!
> 3. The evaluators it scoped were too broad, and bundled too many types of failures at once. This can be avoided with looking at the data first. I'm afraid this might steer people in the wrong direction.
> 4. The workflow put us DEEP into the rabbit hole of a specific eval right away. It also asks "does it look right" at several steps without really giving you enough information to make that determination.
>
> The Good:
>
> 1. I was impressed by the out of the box ability for issue discovery that other auto-eval approaches haven't been able to find! It found issues with human handoff, formatting, voice agents, and more. It's still better to look at your data iteratively with an agent, but this was the strongest performance I've seen with a more "one-shot" issue discovery approach.
> 2. This is a big improvement in terms of UX from their prior eval plugin thing.
> 3. The blog post they released conveys thinking that I agree with, such as the importance of looking at data, sampling intelligently, not saturating your own evals, etc.
>
> Video of our attempt at using this here.
>
> *Quoting @ClaudeDevs:* Claude can now help you build evaluations and hillclimb on them. In this article, we share guidance on eval design & skills that Claude Code can use to improve your applications.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/HamelHusain/status/2104945863084904737
- **Link:** https://claude.dev/blog/automating-eval-design-and-hillclimbing/
- **What:** Hamel Husain tested the claude-api skill's build-eval/hillclimb commands (from Lance Martin's Sep 28 claude.dev playbook on eval design without fooling yourself). Verdict: excellent one-shot issue discovery (human handoff, formatting, voice agents) but it writes evals before error analysis, uses markdown for labeling instead of a custom annotation app, scopes evaluators too broadly, and rushes into one eval.

## @jasonbosco - Two signs of a well-built MCP server: few tools and granular permission scopes
> Signs that an MCP Server is well built:
>
> 1) It thoughtfully limits the number of tools it exposes to the agent (to improve instruction following and reduce context bloat), and instead designs parameters for tool calls.
>
> 2) It separates permission scopes granularly, so that you as a user can choose which actions the agents can take on your behalf. (For eg: separating read vs write for each resource)
>
> Too often, I've seen MCP Servers ship tens of tools with a global read and write permission scope. Makes it totally unusable in real world use cases.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/jasonbosco/status/2104941774406087015
- **What:** MCP server design checklist: expose a small tool set and push variation into parameters to protect context and instruction following, and split read/write scopes per resource. Servers shipping dozens of tools under one global read/write scope are unusable in practice.

## @suraj_sharma14 - 30-point security checklist for vibe-coded apps
> 30 things for Securitymaxxing your vibe coded app:
>
> -  Move every API key out of your frontend
> -  Add .env to .gitignore before your first commit
> -  Rotate any key that ever touched GitHub
> -  Turn on Row Level Security for every table
> -  Never trust the client. Validate on the server
> -  Check auth on every API route not just the UI
> -  Check ownership: can user A read user B's data?
> -  Rate limit login, signup &  password reset
> -  Rate limit your AI endpoints before someone drains your credits
> -  Set hard spending caps on OpenAI, Anthropic & your cloud
> -  Use parameterized queries. No string-built SQL
> -  Sanitize user input before rendering it (XSS)
> -  Lock CORS to your own domains, never "*"
> -  Use HTTPS everywhere with HSTS on
> -  Set secure, httpOnly, sameSite cookies
> -  Hash passwords with bcrypt or argon2 or use a real auth provider
> -  Expire sessions and tokens
> -  Add CSRF protection on state-changing requests
> -  Validate file uploads by type and size & store them outside your app server
> -  Make storage buckets private by default
> -  Verify webhook signatures (Stripe, GitHub, etc.)
> -  Never return stack traces or raw errors to users
> -  Strip secrets and PII from your logs
> -  Run npm audit and update vulnerable packages
> -  Check that the packages your AI suggested actually exist
> -  Guard LLM features against prompt injection
> -  Never let the model run tools or SQL without limits
> -  Add security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options)
> -  Back up your database and test a restore
> - Ask your AI to attack your app before someone else does
>
> Shipping fast is a skill.
> Shipping safe is what keeps you in business.
>
> Bookmark this before your next deploy + send it to a vibe coder.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/suraj_sharma14/status/2104790775397830755
- **What:** Suraj Sharma lists 30 security checks for vibe-coded apps, covering secrets handling, row-level security, server-side validation, rate limits, spending caps, and restore testing. The list targets common AI-generated app failures and ends with a prompt to have the AI attack the app itself.

## @doodlestein - dsr self-hosted builds and the "code first" doctrine for agent swarms
> It seems like lots of people are suddenly realizing that handling builds and tests at scale is now a major bottleneck to high-throughput agent coding.
>
> This is something that I first dealt with late last year when I created MCP Agent Mail and started using a large number of agents at the same time on single projects.
>
> Most of my stuff is open source, so at first I was able to use GitHub Actions for everything, which was convenient. But as the number of projects I was working on skyrocketed, I saw my GitHub Actions usage spike, to the point where it was over $5,000/month of value.
>
> Unsurprisingly, they decided to cut me off after that, so I had to figure something else out. I ended up coming up with my own system called dsr that I've been using since then, which can use the same config files as GitHub Actions, but runs on my own fleet of Linux, Mac, and Windows machines.
>
> You can try it yourself here:
>
> https://t.co/GXzDKKG2Tr
>
> While dsr helped a lot, the bigger problem I realized was that these build/test flows were being used wastefully and way too frequently.
>
> Basically, if you had a swarm of 12 agents all working on the same code base, even if you solved the problems of inter-agent file contention (as I have with the advisory file reservations in my Agent Mail project), you still had to deal with build resource contention, with each agent trying to test and build after each change.
>
> This quickly overwhelms your systems, and again, is totally unnecessary and wasteful. I realized that what you really want is a doctrine that's followed by your swarm, which I refer to as the "code first" doctrine. This is explained in the attached screenshots by Astra.
>
> It's really just common sense, though. And the ideas are thoroughly integrated into my main skill that I use for orchestrating agents using my ntm orchestration tool: /vibing-with-ntm (I also use my /ntm skill to explain the basics of ntm to the agents).
>
> You can get those skills here on my $20/month skills site:
>
> https://t.co/fgcorUVkKn
> https://t.co/m9h9z6CC8G
>
> If you follow this approach, you can save huge amounts of money while still getting the benefits of thorough testing and remote builds.
>
> I've been doing this myself every single day for months across 2,000+ daily commits and dozens of projects, so I know it works at scale.

## @suryaoruganti - Practical Levers for Cutting CI Bills at Scale
> Everyone's posting about how CI bills are exploding.
>
> That's true - here are some practical solutions for teams operating at scale.
>
> - cache heavily.
>
> - use the right sized instance. 2x instance size that reduces runtime by half still costs the same while reducing your wait time. obv not all workloads parallelize well.
>
> - if CI reproducibility isn't important, consider using snapshots or starting from precomputed states for incremental builds. This is why your laptop build feels so much faster than a CI job.
>
> - if building containers, use a heavily cached remote container builder. This is not the same as just uploading cache layers to a remote registry. Speed diff here can be ~10x between the two approaches.
>
> - reduce number of tests. You know you don't care about some of them.
>
> - use @WarpBuilds for faster single core performance and locally connected NVME drives which are the single most important factor for build and test workload performance.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/suryaoruganti/status/2104389894617575524
- **What:** Surya Oruganti lists CI cost fixes: heavy caching, right-sized instances, snapshots or precomputed states, a cached remote container builder, fewer tests, and faster single-core machines with local NVMe such as WarpBuilds. He claims a remote container builder with cache can be about 10x faster than uploading cache layers to a registry.

> Humans tend to like 'sharp knife' abstractions - that are powerful, but you can cut yourself if your use them wrong. Lauren says agents perform much better in extremely locked-down environments. Abstractions are designed so they can't screw up, and lint rules enforce it.
>
> They built a whole internal framework (Dune) to keep the agent on track.
>
> That helps optimise agents that don't have a large context window to work productively in your codebase.
>
> 2. Create verification infrastructure
>
> To trust the results of any agent, you either need to sit and watch it OR have it provide evidence of its improvement. This has always made sense to me, but Lauren really pushes it hard here:
>
> - Invest in custom CLI's that let the agent drive the app and measure its performance
> - Make the app "factory ready" from the get-go - i.e. deployable to an environment where the agent can mess about with it
>
> 3. Feature Maps
>
> Lauren's software factory (what she calls an 'outer loop') often requires the agent to break down vague bug reports from users and to turn those into potential fixes.
>
> To aid that, they built a 'feature map' of all the main features in their application, which describe exactly how the app is supposed to function.
>
> This has become essential for helping the agent navigate the codebase, and figure out quickly how things are supposed to work. It's maintained along with the codebase, and kept in sync via automations.
>
> This is the kind of documentation I usually warn against. It goes stale quickly and can confuse agents if it's not kept up to date.
>
> But Lauren's team are using it as critical navigation infrastructure, and it makes it possible for agents to explore faster and better - even on a large codebase. So it sounds like navigation docs like this are worth it if they enable new behavior. 
>
> Banger talk - watch the whole thing on 2x.
>
> *Quoting @poteto:* here's how i shipped 2,500 PRs last month to production this was originally supposed to be for Cursor Compile in London. i couldn't make it since i was livestreaming for Grok @Bot Galaxy so i'm making it available for free here on X! watch it on 2x speed, i talk slowly https://t.co/NgrGz7tmPM

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/mattpocockuk/status/2103431302527508886
- **Quoted:** https://x.com/poteto/status/2102050467505430555
- **What:** Matt Pocock summarizes Lauren's talk: lock agents into constrained abstractions with lint enforcement, build verification CLIs, and maintain a feature map as navigation infrastructure. Quoted post is the talk itself.

## @RayFernando1337 - Prompt to purge low-signal unit tests and prefer E2E
> I find the latest models write a lot of unit tests. Most of them restate the code they were written after, so they always pass and catch almost nothing. They run fast, but they break on every refactor and the agent burns time fixing tests instead of the feature.
>
> The prompt I used to clean out mine, adopted from Ansh is:
>
> "This repo is full of low-signal unit tests. Delete every one that wouldn't catch a real bug our E2E tests miss. Fan the work out across parallel subagents.
>
> Then add these rules to AGENTS.md so future agents stop writing them.
>
> - Never write unit tests after you write code.
>
> - Highly prefer E2E tests as the sole testing mechanism. Use them to verify complex features work. At the end of E2E tests, produce a verifiable and repeatable artifact.
>
> - If you must test a system in isolation, first write down all the ways it could fail, then write the code."
>
> *Quoting @anshnanda:* At the top of my AGENTS.md: - NEVER write unit tests after you write code.  - Highly prefer E2E tests as the sole testing mechanism. Use them to verify complex features work. At the end of E2E tests, produce a verifiable and repeatable artifact.  - If you must test a system in isolation, FIRST write all the ways it could fail, THEN write the code.

- **What:** Ray Fernando shares a prompt, adapted from Ansh Nanda, that deletes unit tests an E2E suite would not miss via parallel subagents and adds AGENTS.md rules: no tests after code, prefer E2E with artifacts, list failure modes first.

## @FundamentEdge - Where investing alpha moves when public data is priced instantly
> A few thoughts:
>
> 1) if public data is instantly priced, the premium on proprietary, unescapable insights increases. Alpha generation moves entirely to the edges: nuanced management body language, channel checks outside of the Tegus corpus and deep industry relationships.  That has always been true but becomes more true. I think it is obvious public equity investors will spend less time in front of a Bloomberg screen and more time in the field, researching key drivers.
>
> 2). Even more fundamental, capital trust. Being a good fiduciary & steward of capital. Why does one CIO raise $5 billion and another raises zero? Accountability, direct communication, adaptability, judgment during dislocations that ultimately shows up in track record. It is exceedingly hard to completely rewire the investment process of a large investment organization, made harder by the compliance & infosec requirements in place to earn said LP trust (to wit, many large investment organizations are still left with Microsoft CoPilot). It will take years not months to fully shift approach, and very few firms live at the intersection of both leading AI innovation & adaptable infrastructure & talent. You can be fully native and raise no money, and you will have no impact on market price discovery. There will be a window of time where adaptability & urgency as well as the ability to earn trust of capital partners will show up in alpha, in my opinion.
>
> 3) the psychological endurance & judgment required to know when to fade a hyper-efficient consensus. Any consumer PM who has lived through the rise of alternative data will know this dynamic well. When do you ride the machine-generated consensus vs. fade that consensus based on a nuanced variant perception? As in alt data, the game will shift to 2nd & 3rd order thinking. As certain "now-casting" alpha pools compress, certainly other distortions will expand due to positioning, capital flows & narrative over-reactions. These are definitionally alpha opportunities vs. the conceptual intrinsic value baseline (if not difficult, jagged & frustrating to monetize). Call it behavioral resilience and deep intuition around market participants and market price discovery (I am actually quite bullish on vol-adjusted dollar edge, don't think this will be the problem...markets aren't going to wake up in 3 months and all of a sudden be hyper-efficient in price discovery).
>
> *Quoting @LaurelonCapital:* @FundamentEdge Where do you see edge moving?

## @Invested_In_You - In-case-of-death checklist for couples
> I sat with a widow last year. Her husband passed unexpectedly.
>
> She didn't know any of their passwords. Didn't know which accounts existed. Didn't know where the will was.
>
> She wasn't unprepared because they didn't have money.
>
> She was unprepared because they never had the conversation.
>
> Here's the "in case of death" checklist every couple should build together this weekend:
>
> Do this now - before anything happens:
>
> - update beneficiaries on every account - 401k, IRA, life insurance, brokerage
> - add Apple/Google legacy contacts so your spouse can access your phone
> - name accounts jointly wherever possible
> - set autopay on every credit card and bill
> - use a password manager - share access with your spouse today
> - keep your will and trust updated - review every 3-5 years or after any major life event
> - keep a running list of every account, utility, insurance, landscaping, subscription - anything with a payment or login
>
> If your spouse passes:
>
> - call your financial advisor first - they coordinate most of what comes next
> - call your estate planning attorney second
> - get at least 10 certified copies of the death certificate - you'll need more than you think
> - submit the death certificate to every financial institution, insurer, and government agency
> - contact Social Security to report the death and claim any survivor benefit
> - for short term cash needs - start with taxable brokerage accounts first, then IRAs, leave 401ks and Roth accounts for last
>
> Keep one document - updated annually - that includes:
>
> - every account and institution with contact info
> - every autopayment and what card it's on
> - every insurance policy and policy number
> - your advisor, attorney, and CPA contact info
> - where the will, trust, and important documents are physically located
>
> Print it and/or save it to Google Drive.
>
> The greatest gift you can give your family isn't just building wealth.
>
> It's making sure they can access it when they need it most.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/Invested_In_You/status/2102741019704090670
- **What:** Financial checklist after a widow found no passwords, accounts or will: update beneficiaries, set legacy contacts, use a shared password manager, keep an account list and documents, plus steps to take after a spouse dies (advisor, attorney, 10 death certificates, Social Security).

## @RobHoffman_ - About Us page template for AI search and E-E-A-T
> founders and marketers: you need an optimized "about us" page on your site
>
> i work with billion dollar tech companies and bootstrapped SaaS. The About Us is one of the first pages we optimize
>
> here's how (8 points):
>
> (P.S. I explain why this is important at the bottom of the post)
>
> here's how:
>
> 1. start with a clear value prop sentence: "[COMPANY] is a [CATEGORY] that [DOES XYZ] for [ICP]."
>
> 2. add your core services under a "what [COMPANY] does" H2 subheading. Put each service/feature/product in an H3 subheading. Write 2-3 sentences about what you do, and what outcome it produces.
>
> 3. next, add a "what makes [COMPANY] different" H2 subheading. List about 5 core differentiators in H3 subheadings. Give specific, quantifiable differentiators and call out competitors by name. Example: [COMPANY] offers month-to-month payment terms, whereas options like [COMPETITOR] have mandated 12-month contracts. Again: 2-3 sentences per differentiator.
>
> 4. your next H2 should be "who uses [COMPANY]." Add bullet points that call out your exact ICP segments. Example: "B2B SaaS marketing teams at 50 to 200-employees."
>
> 5. now add a "the team behind [COMPANY]" H2 subheading. Include the names of the founders, quick backstories, company origin story, team composition, and links to social pages (especially the founder(s) socials). You only need about 2 sentences per backstory/origin story.
>
> 6. add a "how [COMPANY] works" section. Include info like communication channels, response times, who on the team customers will work with, turnaround time, and onboarding process.
>
> 7. now for the most important section for AI Search: add a "key facts" H2. This should be an HTML <table> or <dl> (definition list) so it's crawlable. Include the following rows:
>
> Company Name
> Type
> Founded
> Founder
> Headquarters
> Website
> Core Offering
> Pricing
> Contract Terms
> Services
> Communication
> Notable Clients
> Customers Served
> Projects Delivered
> Competitors
> Social
>
>  8. finally, add your FAQ section. Put "frequently asked questions" in an H2 subheading with your questions as H3s. Only 2-3 sentences per answer.
>
> Here's why this page is so important:
> 1. it helps train AI to talk about your brand accurately
> 2. it strengthens the E-E-A-T score of your entire domain
> 3. in a world where everything seems fake, make your brand human
>
> shoot me a DM if you want a live demo of the lowest hanging fruit to rank in AI Search (tailored to your specific site)
>
> i hope this helps someone!

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/RobHoffman_/status/2102476527200043250
- **What:** Rob Hoffman gives an 8-part structure for an optimized About Us page (value prop, services, differentiators vs named competitors, ICP, team, process, a crawlable key-facts table, FAQ) to help AI search cite the brand accurately.

## @realfxw - Cloudflare agentic-inbox: self-hosted AI email client on Workers
> Cloudflare 官方开源了一个堪称 Serverless 典范的神级项目：agentic-inbox —— 一个完全跑在 Cloudflare Workers 边缘网络上的自托管 AI 邮件客户端。
>
> 以往自建邮件系统配置繁琐、运维头疼，而这个项目直接将邮件收发、数据存储、UI 界面与 AI Agent 全部打包进了 Cloudflare 生态：
>
> 核心亮点
>
> 纯边缘架构与数据隔离：接入 Cloudflare Email Routing 与 Email Service 搞定邮件收发；每个邮箱独立运行在一个 Durable Object (DO) 中，自带 SQLite 存储邮件，附件则无缝存入 R2，既实现了多租户隔离，又做到了免运维。
>
> 原生 AI Email Agent：基于 Cloudflare Agents SDK 与 Workers AI 构建，内置 9 种邮件处理工具。收到新邮件时，Agent 会自动阅读上下文并起草回复，且严格保留人类确认环节，未经允许绝不私自发信。
>
> 自带 MCP Server 支持：服务原生暴露 /mcp 端点，外部 AI 编程助手（如 Cursor、Claude Code）可以直接挂载该接口，跨工作流读取或处理邮件。
>
> 生产级安全保障：默认集成 Cloudflare Access JWT 验证，防止个人邮箱系统暴露在公网，零配置实现企业级访问控制。
>
> 技术栈速览
>
> 前端：React 19、React Router v7、Tailwind CSS、TipTap 编辑器、Zustand
>
> 后端与存储：Hono、Cloudflare Workers、Durable Objects (SQLite)、R2
>
> AI 驱动：Cloudflare Agents SDK (AIChatAgent)、AI SDK v6、Workers AI
>
> 如果你正在探索 Workers 全家桶的工程化实践，或者想给自己的域名搭一个兼顾隐私与自动化能力的专属邮件中心，这个开源实现是极具参考价值的标杆案例。
>
> 🔗 源码传送门：https://t.co/PiZdA0l4Bm

## @kunchenguid - Jev replaces LLM dispatch routing in firstmate orchestrator
> alright - just got Jev deployed for a real production use case, which now performs at fable level quality but 10x faster and saves a ton of money
>
> context - a powerful capability of firstmate is that as an orchestrator it intelligently routes each task to an appropriate agent (permutation of harness, model, and reasoning effort) based on custom user preference
>
> by default, that's done by the firstmate agent and the LLM would have to do some thinking, make tool calls to read dispatch rules, quota data etc and then do the dispatch. this is slow and does cost a bit of LLM tokens
>
> i just replaced this dispatch process with Jev. it makes the same decision with no thinking or tool calls, done in ~200ms, and for the 25 tasks i evaluated this with, it gives the exact same answer fable would have given... 
>
> there's still a tool call needed to invoke Jev, done by the firstmate agent which uses an LLM. but even with that counted, the saving from Jev still resulted in a -71% reduction in cost and -90% reduction in wall time of completing the whole dispatching process
>
> Jev API calls themselves are almost free.. i made 100+ calls, and my usage dashboard still shows $0.01 (which i think means "haven't reached $0.01 yet"). if we just look at the part Jev replaced and not the whole system, then the saving is on the magnitude of ~100x
>
> if you also have Jev and you use firstmate, set TYPESAFE_API_KEY in your .env file in your firstmate repo to activate this
>
> exciting times! i think this is starting to enable a whole new architectural paradigm for software. LLMs are just a small part of it. more on that soon

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/kunchenguid/status/2100468943853085061
- **What:** Kun Chen swapped firstmate's LLM-based agent dispatch for Jev: about 200ms per decision, matched Fable's answer on all 25 evaluated tasks, cutting whole-process cost 71% and wall time 90%. Argues cheap decision models enable a new software architecture.

## @srishticodes - Tech hiring tests solved problems, real jobs need problem discovery
> Modern tech hiring is funny.

> anyway reverse this linked list.

- **What:** Satirical critique of algorithm-style interviews: they test well-specified puzzles, while real engineering work is ambiguous, undocumented debugging where defining the problem is half the job.

> Qwen3.8-27B just got a lot more interesting for Mac users.
> 
> You can now run the vision version of Qwen3.8-27B locally on a 16GB Mac using MLX.
> 
> That is a pretty big deal for local AI.
> 
> The full model is far too large for a 16GB machine in its original form, but the new quantized versions range from 29.5GB down to just 11.8GB.
> 
> That puts the smaller builds within reach of Macs with limited unified memory.
> 
> The standout is:
> 
> AD 3.50bpw DWQ
> → 12.7GB
> → Vision support
> → 27B parameters
> → MLX local inference
> → 79.6% next-token agreement with the original BF16 model
> 
> That last number is especially interesting.
> 
> Quantization isn’t just about making a model smaller. The real challenge is reducing memory usage without destroying the model’s behavior.
> 
> Getting a 27B vision model down to roughly 12.7GB while retaining the same next-token choice as the BF16 model nearly 80% of the time shows how far these techniques have come.
> 
> And because Apple Silicon uses unified memory, you don’t have the traditional VRAM vs system RAM split you deal with on discrete GPUs.
> 
> So the practical takeaway is simple:
> 
> A 16GB Mac can now run a 27B vision model locally.
> 
> No cloud inference.
> 
> No API calls.
> 
> No dedicated GPU required.
> 
> Just Apple Silicon, MLX, and a heavily optimized quant.
>

> 
> The model is running locally on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395, and I was mainly curious about two things:
> 
> Can a local 27B model actually handle a real Blender workflow?
> How painful would the token generation speed be on this hardware?
> 
> The second one surprised me.
> 
> Token generation is considerably faster than I expected.
> 
> That matters because Blender tasks aren’t just about generating a few lines of Python. A serious 3D workflow can involve creating geometry, setting materials, arranging objects, adding modifiers, building scenes, checking the result, and iterating when something looks wrong.
> 
> A model that can generate and refine those steps quickly starts becoming genuinely useful as a local 3D assistant.
> 
> And because Qwen3.8-27B is running locally, the entire workflow stays on the machine.
> 
> No cloud API.
> 
> No uploading project files.
> 
> No waiting on a remote model for every Blender operation.
> 
> The interesting experiment now is seeing how far this can go.
> 
> Can it build complete scenes?
> 
> Can it create detailed procedural geometry?
> 
> Can it work with Blender’s Python API reliably?
> 
> Can it inspect its own results and fix mistakes?
> 
> If the generation speed keeps holding up, Qwen3.8-27B + Blender on Ryzen AI Max+ is looking like a capable local 3D workflow. https://t.co/dkFV8BAcH1

## @analogalok - Qwen 3.8 27B dense runs on 8GB VRAM laptop, beats cloud models on agentic index
> Look at this leaderboard very carefully.
> 
> Qwen 3.8 27B (dense) is outranking GPT 5.6 Terra and DeepSeek V4 Pro on the Artificial Analysis Agentic Index (51 score).
> 
> And you can run this exact model on a $300, 8GB VRAM gaming laptop (RTX 4060, 3070, 5050, 5060, 2060 super, 2070 super etc.) at 5+ tokens/sec, running on a battery!
> 
> Let that sink in. A model beating frontier cloud models is running on budget consumer silicon without OOMing. Small quantization tax with IQ4_XS compared to the FP16 test run, but the performance to VRAM ratio is still insane.
> 
> If this is where we are today, where are we in 6 months? Opus 5 level agentic intelligence running fully offline on an 8GB GPU? It’s not an if, it’s a when.
> 
> Copy/paste llama.cpp flags to run it on 8GB right now:
> 
> .\llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-IQ4_XS.gguf -c 64000 --port 8080 -ngl 25 -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 --threads 6 --threads-batch 8 --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 --spec-draft-p-min 0.7
> 
> Grab @UnslothAI's Hugging Face GGUF in the first reply
>
> *Quoting @analogalok:* Running Qwen 3.8 27B Q4 on a single RTX 4060 (8GB VRAM) gaming laptop shouldn’t be physically possible.
> 
> You can now run this 27B dense beast locally with a massive 64,000 token context window (minimum requirement by hermes agent) on budget consumer hardware, without crashing into OOM hell.
> 
> A model that bests claude opus 4.6 in several benchmarks, now runs on a $300 GPU!
> 
> after benchmarking it on rtx 4090 (24 GB VRAM) yesterday, today i tested on an Intel i7 12700H rig with an 8GB VRAM card and only 16GB dual channel DDR4 RAM, PCIe 4.  
> 
> The breakthrough is using the new IQ4_XS quant by Unsloth (occupies just 14.6 GB on disk vs 16.7 GB for standard Q4_K_XL). 
> 
> By tuning hybrid CPU/GPU offloading and quantized KV cache, we unlocked deep context with usable generation speeds.  
> 
> Here are the numbers from a 4.5k real world prompt test: 
> 
> - Context Window: 64,000 tokens (-c 64000) 
> - Prefill Speed: 150 tokens/sec 
> - Decode Speed: 5 tokens/sec (steady generation via native MTP) 
> 
> The exact llama.cpp flags to run it right now:  
> 
> .\llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-IQ4_XS.gguf -c 64000 --port 8080 -ngl 25 -ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0 --threads 6 --threads-batch 8 --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 --spec-draft-p-min 0.7 
> 
> this occupies the vram completely.
> 
> Why this works: 
> 
> 1. `-ngl 25` offloads just enough layers to fill your 8GB VRAM without memory spillover. 
> 
> 2. `-ctk q4_0 -ctv q4_0` crushes the KV cache memory footprint. 
> 
> 3. Native MTP (`draft-mtp`) drafts candidate tokens ahead to keep CPU bound decode at a readable pace.  
> 
> Complete stress test benchmark suite for this setup drops tomorrow.  
> 
> Unsloths's Hugging Face GGUF link in the replies.
> 
> fire it up on your 8GB rig tonight. What budget GPU are you testing this on?

> It's actually crazy watching everyone pivot in the complete wrong direction from what companies want. Having an army of agents/bots is counterproductive. It's a vanity metric. ## @1adrianpierce - Recipe for front-loaded PRD-to-beads planning sessions in an agent software factory
> recipe for successful PLANNING sessions in your software factory:
>
> - use fable
> - describe the rough shape of what you want to build in as much detail as possible (dictation works great)
> - have fable pressure test/grill you in batches of questions
> - dispatch research subagents (opus is fine) to ground or disprove ideas with evidence
> - draft or update a PRD (context, goals, non-goals, success criteria, journeys, requirements, architecture decisions, data model, contracts, security/failure modes, open questions)
> - read and review the PRD (don't skip this)
> - set project-level testing and documentation cadence and policies
> - decompose the PRD into detailed technical tasks (beads) optimized for maximum parallelism, each with clear acceptance criteria
> - dispatch subagents for adversarial review of tasks and PRD mapping
>
> planning like this is hard and takes a long time - and that's the point, you are heavily front-loading the work. if you do this, your factory should be able to reliably execute very large batches of work either completely or mostly unattended (escalations/blockers only)

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/1adrianpierce/status/2087919654618497304
- **What:** Step-by-step planning workflow: dictate the idea, get grilled by the model, research with subagents, write and review a PRD, set policies, split into parallel beads, then adversarial review. Heavy upfront planning lets implementation run mostly unattended.

## @ipwanciu - HTTP QUERY method (RFC 10008): safe, idempotent, cacheable GET with a body
> That's a small reminder! 👇 As of June 2026, there's a new HTTP method - a GET with `body` 😎 Meet QUERY (RFC 10008). Browsers are still adding full support, usable now with care, widespread adoption coming later in 2026+.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/ipwanciu/status/2087226776523092390
- **What:** HTTP QUERY (RFC 10008) allows request bodies for complex reads while remaining safe, idempotent and cacheable, fixing the GET-URL-length versus POST-semantics tradeoff. Server frameworks support it; browser support is still arriving.

Revenue schedule / Gantt chart tabs with revenue recognition and contracted revenue over time. Summary / settings tabs. We made ours in Google Sheets with Claude!
>
> 2/ PL_Memo_0226: Your memo serves a different purpose than your deck. Its job is to tell a story and sell a vision. Sections: Who we are, our niche and bet, market / competition, execution, and team. Ours was 1 page.
>
> 3/ PL_Deck_0226: Team, product differentiation, comp landscape, traction, win rate / pipeline, case studies. Invest in design!!!
>
> 4/ Operating_Model: Usually the hardest for early stage companies. But great if you can show operating margins. It communicates seriousness if you understand your costs and investments, and are thoughtful about how you project them to grow. This helps answer the question "Why do you need $5M instead of $2M"
>
> 5/ Pipeline_ALL: Include closed won, closed lost, and all other pipeline stages. How the customer found you, projected deal value, etc. (historic included)

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/sfakkawi/status/2085369956812693839
- **What:** Founder playbook for a seed data room: customer/contract cube spreadsheet, a one-page narrative memo, a designed deck, an operating model that justifies the raise size, and a full historical pipeline. Claims this got a seed raised in 5 days at an 80th percentile valuation.

## @mstockton - Good skills are terse: lesson from Matt Pocock's /wait-what
> I like reading (and sometimes using) common SKILLs libraries. Some are fantastic, like the collection from @mattpocockuk
>
> It's worth noting that the *entire* skill text for this new 'wait-what' is:
>
> 'Wait — I don't understand where you've got to here. Re-pitch that: give me a little bit of context, talk in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English, and use the ubiquitous language from `CONTEXT.md`.'
>
> It's not complex. It's very few words. It's terse and to the point, as it should be.
>
> So what is the take-away? It's actually not that difficult to create valuable skills that give you incredible leverage. You just need to:

> 2. Describe it simply and directly

> - 在充分满足当前需求的前提下，采用尽可能简单的实现方案。避免缺乏依据的抽象、配置项和间接层。
> - 采用渐进式、分层的方式构建系统。先完成端到端运行的最小版本，再逐步增加功能。
> - 保持组件的模块化，明确划分职责。
> - 成熟且维护良好的库能降低复杂度时应优先采用，不重复实现通用功能。
> - 新增依赖或自行实现前，先评估现有依赖的能力，查阅文档和类型定义。
> - 架构决策着眼长期演进，不采用预期会被替换的权宜方案。
> - 设计方案前先研究成熟产品如何解决同类问题，优先采用经过验证的模式。

## @fin465 - Outbound GTM rules: deliverability hygiene, signal-based triggers, and mining closed-won/churned/competitor data
> "GTM iS EaSY"
>
> GTM:
> > turn off open tracking
> > no link in the first email, ever
> > never send from your root domain
> > verify emails at send, not at import
> > 30 sends a day per mailbox, no more
> > plain text, no images, no tracking pixels
> > score positive replies, not total replies
> > waterfall three data providers, never trust one
> > enrich your tier one accounts, not the whole list
> > use local data providers for emea and apac lists
> > don't discard catch-alls, score them and send anyway
> > track headcount deltas by department, not by company
> > filter the list by mx record before you write any copy
> > funding rounds are the most spammed signal in outbound
> > 300 contacts per variant or you are just reading noise
> > a first sales ops hire beats a series b as a trigger
> > rebuild the list monthly, a third of titles rot every year
> > a job post naming your competitor is a displacement signal
> > read their job posts for the tech stack, it beats builtwith
> > two customers asking for the same integration is a channel
> > ai personalization on a bad list only amplifies the bad list
> > write the first email to be forwarded down, not read at the top
> > champion job changes are your warmest list and they cost nothing
> > target whoever owns the pain, then ask them who owns the budget
> > measure at meetings held, everything upstream of that is a proxy
> > a new vp has 90 days to swap vendors, that window is your campaign
> > soc2 on their trust center means they just started selling upmarket
> > export closed-won, enrich it, and find the three attributes every account shares that your icp doc never mentions
> > find where the champions from your last 20 lost deals work now, and open with the workflow you already know they run
> > pull your competitor's sitemap, grab /customers and /case-studies, enrich every logo you find, that's the best list you'll ever build
> > scrape every job post that names your competitor, filter to the last 30 days, and send the displacement email to the hiring manager, not the recruiter
> > take your churned power users, find their new employers, and open with the exact workflow they used to run, nobody else hitting their inbox knows that

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/fin465/status/2083259166337196169
- **What:** A dense checklist of cold-outbound practices: strict deliverability (no tracking, low volume per mailbox, secondary domains), verify and waterfall data, measure meetings held. ## @ankrgyl - Behavior specs: open standard for grading agents on how they should behave, not just their output
> I have long felt the diminishing effectiveness of LLM-as-a-judge for agents, and one day over coffee @mitch_troy gave me a rant that helped clarify why. The ground truth for an agent isn't its output, it is how the agent should behave.
>
> This is important for two reasons: 
>
> (1) it is very difficult to generate good ground truth values
>
> (2) to effectively debug why an agent produced invalid outputs, you need to introspect its behavior. 
>
> Mitch then walked through why this is so hard for their team's tax agents. The behaviors themselves are subtle, hard-earned lessons from analyzing lots of failures in their traces in Braintrust, and to effectively flag them, you must effectively document them.
>
> That discussion led us to build behavior specs: a new open standard we're releasing with @trybasis that documents how agents should behave. The repo includes a definition of the spec along with open examples for how to write good specs, evaluate agents using it, and more.
>
> Clear, human-articulated prose is the highest leverage way to drive agentic systems to produce great outcomes. Behavior specs provide a framework to do that with evals. I'm super excited to work on this in the open, and would love to get feedback from others on how we can make this spec maximally useful.
>
> Please try it out, and share your thoughts!
>
> *Quoting @mitch_troy:* Out of the box, long-horizon agents struggle to accurately perform end to end work in the real economy (outside of coding) because those tasks are not easily verifiable, the data is hard to scale, and going from inputs to real outcomes can actually take many days.
>
> Even if you had a reliable way to verify outcomes at scale (and weren’t bothered by the multi-hour iteration loops), the sheer volume of decisions by the agent that occur in a multi-hour job makes it hard to know whether performing well will generalize to production.
>
> Over the last two years at @trybasis, we've been solving this problem by supervising the process our agents take to get to outcomes, rather than just looking at whether the outcome itself is correct.
>
> We think this is the key to building production agents at scale. 
>
> It's what has allowed us to run agents in production that operate for hours, sometimes days, and reliably perform tasks like entire complex tax returns end to end.
>
> Today, alongside @braintrust, we're open sourcing a standard for defining, evaluating, and eventually rewarding agent behaviors.
>
> Thread below with all the details on how we’re scaling behaviors to close the loop for long-horizon agents.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/ankrgyl/status/2082565187064811637
- **Quoted:** https://x.com/mitch_troy/status/2082513195357307158
- **Link:** https://www.agentbehavior.dev/
- **What:** Braintrust and Basis release an open spec (BEHAVIOR.md files under .agents/behaviors/) that documents expected agent behavior across repeated interactions. Premise: for long-horizon agents, ground truth is process, not output, so evals and trace review should check behaviors instead of relying on LLM-as-judge on outputs.

## @mitchellh - ChatGPT automation finds $45K in erroneous construction invoices
> A ChatGPT automation just found ~$45K in erroneous invoices across 3 years of billing history that I've confirmed and already had resolved. My lifetime history for ChatGPT is ~$1,800, so it just paid for itself 25x over.
>
> I setup an automation with read-only access to my email, and tasked this one specifically with analyzing construction invoices. It has access to prior construction invoices, emails, meeting notes, etc. It produces a report and emails it to me (the only email its allowed to send, enforced by API token) whenever I receive a construction invoice.
>
> Across 3 years of construction projects, it found about $45K in issues. Some were wrong amounts, some were duplicate invoices, some were invoices addressed to the wrong person. I manually verified, emailed my GCs, and got refunded/credited.
>
> I get multiple construction bills each month and each bill is ~50 pages in a PDF of low-quality scanned paper. I do manually review each bill but its pretty hard to be right all the time.
>
> I do believe these were genuine mistakes and not done out of ill will just based on what the mistakes were. I don't want to share my full construction costs across the past few years, but $45K is a very small percentage of overall billed amounts.
>
> Pretty sweet.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/mitchellh/status/2077053324835389497
- **What:** Mitchell Hashimoto describes a narrowly scoped ChatGPT automation with read-only email access that reviews scanned construction invoices against history, and found about $45K of errors (wrong amounts, duplicates, wrong addressee) that were refunded. It is a concrete pattern for safe agent automation: least-privilege access, a single API-token-enforced output channel, and domain-specific context.

> There is a massive demand for processing files *in the agent loop*. The number of users submitting agent queries with file attachments is exponentially increasing over time.

## @PawelHuryn - CLAUDE.md delegation and escalation block cuts token cost 5x
> I reduced token cost 5x with a single CLAUDE.md block. Opus is the default parent. It can escalate to Fable: ## Delegation - the higher the tier, the more you delegate. Push work down, keep your own context for judgment. Brief the child: context, why, what done looks like. A child starts blank and inherits nothing. | Haiku | bulk mechanical | never | low | ...
>
> *Quoting @PawelHuryn:* Fable 5 is back, where work runs matters again. Delegation pushes work down to cheaper models. The move almost nobody uses: escalation, one step up. Top tiers hand work down to save themselves for judgment calls. Cheaper models just do the work. The main cost lever is which model runs where. The parent doesn't have to be the top model. An Opus parent can spawn a Fable child for a single hard call and keep the rest on Opus. The child answers and returns. It never escalates on its own. Over-tier work goes back to the parent, one step up.

- **What:** Pawel shares a CLAUDE.md block with a model-tier table (Haiku bulk work at low effort, Sonnet scoped research, Opus 4.8 multi-step reasoning, Fable 5 judgment at medium, xhigh only for hardest calls). ## @afshineemrani - Cardiologist: inflammation, not just LDL, drives heart attacks; tests and treatments to ask about
> I'm a cardiologist. I've held dying hearts in my hands in the cath lab at 3 AM. And I need to tell you something that changes everything about how we prevent heart attacks.
>
> For decades, the entire field was built on one target: lower LDL cholesterol. Statins save lives — that's settled science. But too many of my patients did everything right — took their statins, hit their numbers, lived clean — and still ended up on my table with a ruptured artery.
>
> We were treating the smoke while the fire kept burning.
> The fire is inflammation. And the evidence is now overwhelming.
>
> The CANTOS trial proved it first — lowering inflammation independent of cholesterol reduced cardiac events. But the newer data is what keeps me up at night.
>
> AI-enhanced CT angiography can now detect inflamed arteries by measuring changes in the fat surrounding your coronary vessels — the perivascular fat attenuation index. Higher inflammation in the fat around even one artery independently predicts cardiac death. When multiple arteries show inflammation, the risk multiplies dramatically — even in patients whose cholesterol looks perfect.
>
> This isn't theoretical. This is measurable. Right now. On a scan you can get this month.
>
> Low-dose colchicine — a drug that's been around for centuries for gout — is now FDA-approved specifically for reducing cardiovascular events. It works by quieting the inflammatory cascade that destabilizes the plaque sitting in your arteries. A pill that costs pennies is saving lives the statins couldn't reach.
>
> And the next wave is already in Phase 3 trials. Ziltivekimab — an IL-6 inhibitor — targets the central inflammatory pathway driving atherosclerosis. Phase 2 data showed a 90% reduction in hsCRP. The ZEUS cardiovascular outcomes trial is enrolling now, with results expected late 2026 into 2027. If positive, anti-inflammatory therapy will become standard in managing heart disease alongside lipid-lowering. The era of inflammation-targeted cardiology is arriving.
> But it goes deeper than drugs. AI is now predicting heart failure and cardiac events 5+ years before symptoms — integrating CT imaging, electronic health records, and genetic data with accuracy that jumps far beyond traditional risk calculators.
>
> And polygenic risk scores — a simple genetic test that flags inherited cardiovascular risk — are now formally recognized as a risk-enhancing factor in the 2026 ACC/AHA guidelines. A single blood draw can reveal risk that's been silently building since birth. Decades before the first chest pain.
>
> Here's what this means for you right now — today:
> Ask your doctor for a high-sensitivity CRP test. It's cheap, routine, and measures the systemic inflammation that standard cholesterol panels completely miss. You can have perfect LDL and inflamed arteries that are quietly preparing to rupture.
> If your hsCRP is elevated, discuss low-dose colchicine with your physician. It's FDA-approved for exactly this.
> Push for a coronary CT angiography with AI plaque and inflammation analysis if you have risk factors. This isn't the stress test your parents got. This is 3D visualization of your actual arteries — with AI quantifying not just how much plaque you have, but what kind it is and whether the surrounding tissue is inflamed.
> Consider polygenic risk score testing — especially with a family history of early heart disease. It's now guideline-supported.
>
> And the foundation that never changes: move daily, eat real food, sleep 7-9 hours, manage stress, and know your numbers — ApoB, Lp(a), hsCRP, fasting insulin.
> I left Iran as a child with nothing. I rebuilt everything in a country that gave me the freedom to become a physician. I've spent twenty years watching patients get second chances.
>
> The ones who haunt me aren't the ones who died on my table. They're the ones who survived but never acted on what the science was telling them — years before the event that didn't have to happen.
>
> You can have perfect cholesterol and still have a heart attack. Inflammation plus genetics can drive plaque rupture in arteries that look "fine" on a standard panel.
> The myth that normal cholesterol means you're safe has cost more lives than I can count.
>
> We now have the tools to detect the fire — not just the smoke. AI to see it. Genetics to predict it. Drugs to quiet it. And the ancient basics — movement, real food, sleep, purpose — to prevent it from starting.
>
> Prevention is the new cure. And the science to make it real is no longer coming.
> It's here.

- **What:** Cardiologist argues residual cardiovascular risk comes from arterial inflammation that LDL panels miss. Points to CANTOS, AI-read CT perivascular fat index, low-dose colchicine, IL-6 inhibitor ziltivekimab (ZEUS trial), polygenic risk scores, and asks readers to request hsCRP, ApoB, and Lp(a) tests. ## @doodlestein - Fuzzing skill for parsers: 780M-call campaign on SEC Form 3/4/5 Rust parser
> If you're making software that is designed to parse complex, diverse data, especially when YOU don't control the data, and it is generated in varied ways by thousands of different organizations or users, then there's really no substitute for what's known as "fuzzing" tests.
>
> Fuzzing is a testing technique where you try to intelligently generate a huge number of varied inputs to your program, with the goal of finding parsing bugs that you'd be unlikely to come across if you're only testing with a fixed set of valid inputs.
>
> A naive approach to generating random inputs would be wasteful, since most inputs are trivially invalid and can be quickly rejected.
>
> What you really want are inputs that are pathological; ones that are nearly valid but have some bizarre issue that can confuse your parsing rules and trigger code pathways that you'd normally never traverse.
>
> Fuzzing used to be a somewhat esoteric approach used by security-focused engineers in high-stakes, sophisticated applications. But now anyone can use it. I have a skill specifically for fuzzing you can try here:
>
> https://jeffreys-skills.md/skills/testing-fuzzing
>
> It's part of a series of testing-related skills that also includes metamorphic testing, conformance harness testing, golden artifact generation, end-to-end integration testing, etc.
>
> The skill works across many popular languages and automatically installs the needed tooling for you, instruments your application for fuzzing, and then mounts extended fuzz testing campaigns.
>
> You can see an example of one in the screenshot, where it's been working for many hours, subjecting three different parsers in my hedge_fund_data_tool to torture tests.
>
> For instance, my elaborate parser for SEC insider trade forms (i.e., Forms 3, 4, and 5), which is thousands of lines of Rust, has been called over 780 million times, each invocation with a different, optimally selected input designed to best explore all the different possible code paths within the parser.
>
> There aren't that many forms of this kind in the history of the SEC's EDGAR database, across all companies. The only way to do something like that is with fuzzing. And now you can!

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/doodlestein/status/2064039780971917408
- **Link:** https://jeffreys-skills.md/skills/testing-fuzzing
- **What:** Argues fuzzing (near-valid pathological inputs) is the only way to harden parsers for data you do not control, and promotes his agent skill that installs tooling, instruments code, and runs long campaigns. Evidence cited: a Rust SEC Form 3/4/5 parser exercised 780M+ times; the skill is one of a testing series (metamorphic, conformance, golden, e2e).

> C3, our youngest, started on TimeBack about 20-30 minutes a day this week.

>
> Once C3 got into the actual learning, it got a lot better.

>

>
> For fast math, the Alpha Numbers App is great. There is a lot of recognition of numbers and training for faster calculation and coming up with answers quickly. C3 is having a lot of fun with it, even when the volume of things to be done is a lot.
>
> For reading fluency, the learning loop involves speaking into a microphone to give the Alpha app answers. I have to be there and point to C3 to start answering at the right time. > Everything works, except that without me there 1:1, it would be very difficult to have C3 stay on task for enough time to make progress.

## @doodlestein - Multi-model weighted soft-dimension scoring turns fuzzy problems into an optimizable loss
> This is a really useful trick. LLMs are uniquely good at generating scores for attributes in a repeatable, consistent way.
>
> And if you want the scores to be robust, you can use multiple models and average each sub-score, with a penalty for when they diverge a lot between models.
>
> *Quoting @doodlestein:* @ryancarson You can define a multi-factor scoring system across various "soft" dimensions (e.g., an "elegance" score between 0 and 1,000) that gets rolled into a single weighted overall score and suddenly make just about any problem have a numerical loss factor that you can optimize over.

- **Quoted:** https://x.com/doodlestein/status/2060778023566098842
- **Tweet:** https://x.com/doodlestein/status/2060788830462968239
- **What:** Define LLM-scored soft dimensions (e.g. elegance 0-1000), roll them into one weighted score, and treat it as a loss function to optimize. For robustness, average sub-scores across several models and penalize cross-model disagreement.

## @garrytan - SkillOpt paper: treating SKILL.md files as trainable parameters, plus Garry's "skillify" tip
> This sounds complicated but the agents can implement this in OpenClaw/Hermes Agent trivially (use skillify from GBrain with a link to this tweet)
>
> Sounds ridiculous but you should try it
>
> *Quoting @muratcan:* Gradient descent for SKILL.md files sounds interesting, maybe a bit complex but it's becoming a real part of agent harness. SkillOpt is one of the first papers to treat markdown skill files as trainable parameters and provides a proper optimization framework for them. Lessons: (1) validation gate on held-out set with strict improvement is the only thing that matters, best skills land with 1-4 accepted edits; (2) bounded edits (4-8 per step) beat full rewrites; (3) compact skills win, median ~920 tokens; (4) a Codex-trained skill ported to Claude Code gained +59.7 points on SpreadsheetBench; (5) frozen model + trained context is the practical adaptation; (6) verification is the bottleneck for open-ended work. Also notes a protected-section invariant keeping fast edits from overwriting slow lessons (worth 22 points).

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/garrytan/status/2059144022778896392
- **Quoted:** https://x.com/muratcan/status/2059113412278227328
- **Link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.23904
- **What:** Garry Tan says agents can implement SkillOpt-style skill optimization trivially by running GBrain's skillify against the thread. Murat's summary of the paper (SkillOpt: Executive Strategy for Self-Evolving Agent Skills) gives practical rules: strict held-out validation gates, capped edit size, compact skills, and protected slow-state sections.

## @browomo - Obsidian vault that auto-ingests and surfaces trading ideas via Claude and n8n
> This Chinese guy built a Second Brain in Obsidian and every morning gets 3 trading ideas that brought him $180,000 in 6 months. Inside he runs a pipeline of 6 workflows on N8N that automatically pulls every read article, listened podcast, and voice note into a shared Obsidian vault, and a neural network analyst every morning at 6:00 finds connections between the fresh and the old and puts the 3 strongest trading ideas for the day into the inbox. No analytics desk, no Bloomberg terminal, no Telegram chats with traders. Just a Mac Mini by the wall, an iPhone in the pocket, and 1 local Obsidian vault. And traditional quant funds keep entire teams of 8 people on salary for the same flow of insights, while his expenses are only subscriptions to Readwise, Whisper API, and N8N hosting. 6 pipelines process about 200 sources a day and close the monthly API bill at about $120. The Mac Mini itself stores the entire vault and keeps the neural network analyst running 24/7, and from the iPhone the owner drops any idea he hears on the go into a Telegram bot, and it lands in the vault inbox in just 30 seconds. The starting instruction that sits in the VAULT.md file at the root of his vault looks like this: "you are the AI analyst of a solo trader. you read his vault every morning at 6:00, find connections between fresh and old notes, and deliver 3 trading ideas he can verify in the hour before the market opens. pipelines: // Reader (pulls every article and highlight from Readwise, Twitter bookmarks, and Kindle into /notes) // Listener (transcribes podcasts through Airr and voice notes through Whisper, puts them in /notes) // Catcher (accepts any message from the Telegram bot and writes it to /inbox with a timestamp) // Connector (every night reads across the entire vault and updates the connection graph between 4,000 notes) // Briefer (at 6:00 AM writes a brief: 3 trading ideas for today plus the emerging thesis of the week, puts it in /inbox) // Mobile (lives in the iPhone, answers any question about the vault by voice, and confirms alerts while the owner is on the go). you wake the owner with a push notification only when a fresh note contradicts his active thesis or when 1 of the 3 morning ideas has a confidence score above 90%." This instruction immediately sets the role for the system and the limits of its autonomy. It knows it is supposed to connect new with old on its own. It knows it is supposed to prepare 3 trading ideas every morning on its own. It knows it connects the live trader only when a thesis is contradicted or an ultra-confident idea appears. → Reader pulls about 80 articles and highlights a day from Readwise, Twitter, and Kindle → Listener transcribes 4 to 6 podcasts a week through Airr and Whisper → Catcher intercepts all voice and text ideas through the Telegram bot, averaging 15 to 20 a day → Connector updates the connection graph between 4,000 notes every night, adding 25 to 30 new edges → Briefer puts a fresh brief with 3 trading ideas and the emerging thesis into the inbox at exactly 6:00 → Mobile answers any question about the vault by voice and confirms alerts right from the iPhone And only when a new note contradicts his active thesis or 1 of the ideas breaks 90% confidence does the orchestrator raise the owner with a push notification. And when the trader at that moment is driving to the gym or eating breakfast, the Mobile agent in his iPhone answers any quick question about the vault by voice: what he wrote about this ticker last week, which 3 sources support the idea of long NVDA, and what counter-thesis already sits in his notes. The trader makes the decision and sends the order before New York opens. The fresh brief from last Monday looks like this: "reader: 78 materials added over the weekend, 11 of them about semiconductors, 4 about energy, 3 about biotech. passing to connector." "connector: 27 new connections found between fresh materials and the vault, the strongest one is that the Goldman report from Wednesday matches the NVDA thesis you wrote 3 weeks ago." "briefer: 3 trading ideas for today: long NVDA (confidence 0.84), short Tesla at the close of the quarterly report (0.71), watch URI (0.62). emerging thesis of the week: the market is underpricing capex on data centers." "alert: your fresh note about long-term risk in semis contradicts the NVDA thesis. sending for review." In his work setup there is no cloud server, no team of analysts, and not even a Bloomberg subscription. At home sits a Mac Mini with a local Obsidian vault, on top run 6 N8N pipelines and a neural network analyst, and the same vault mirrors to a secure terminal on the iPhone. Out of everything I have seen this year, this is the cleanest solo trading setup on a second brain: $120 a month on the API, about $30,000 a month into the account, and between them 6 pipelines, 4,000 connected notes, and 1 iPhone in the pocket.

## @levelsio - levelsio secures VPS with Cloudflare Tunnel plus Tailscale, no inbound ports
> New fun thing I did to secure my VPS even further I installed @Cloudflare Tunnel, many of you recommended me this I already had 443 inbound firewall limited to Cloudflare's IP range, but this is even better Cloudflare Tunnel is outbound, which means it connects from your server to Cloudflare, and keeps the connection active, then if someone opens your site, Cloudflare sends you the package via the tunnel and your server responds Then you can block ALL inbound traffic on your firewall (in my case the Hetzner firewall in the dashboard), so now NOBODY can ever access my server, only Cloudflare and Tailscale (which is my own subnet which just my server and my laptop on it) You can just ask AI to set it up on the server etc., very easy
>
> *Quoting @levelsio:* When I set up a new Hetzner VPS first thing I do install Tailscale and once I'm in via Tailscale lock down the firewall to only accept web traffic on HTTPS 443 for Cloudflare IPs and SSH 22 for Tailscale IP That way nobody can get in I know I keep repeating this but it should be basics of setting up a new VPS So basic IMHO it should be part of any VPS service to default install Tailscale and enable it so it's the only way to get in Why? A VPS server is just like your laptop or destop computer but now imagine if it's connected to the entire internet with 8 billion people that can access it and try hack it You want to only have it accessible to you And if you want to host a website on your VPS (like I do), you should only let Cloudflare access your VPS so it can stand in front and block any hack attempts Never expose a VPS to the world wide web which realistically is the world WILD web

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/levelsio/status/2052033385778823436
- **What:** Follow-up to his earlier Tailscale + Cloudflare-IP firewall setup: Cloudflare Tunnel makes the connection outbound, so all inbound traffic can be blocked at the Hetzner firewall, leaving only Cloudflare and Tailscale access. Quoted post is the original baseline hardening recipe.

## @k1rallik - Chrome silently downloads 4GB Gemini Nano weights.bin model
> do you understand what just happened to your computer.. Google Chrome secretly downloaded a 4GB AI model onto your device. Without asking.. Without telling you.. It's called weights.bin. It lives deep in your system folders. It powers Gemini Nano - Google's on-device AI. And if you delete it? Chrome re-downloads it automatically. Like nothing happened. Just Google deciding your hard drive is their storage unit. At 1 billion Chrome users - that's 4 BILLION gigabytes of data pushed silently across the internet. The carbon footprint alone equals tens of thousands of cars running for a year. Check your disk right now: 📁 %LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User Data\OptGuideOnDeviceModel To stop it: chrome://flags → disable Optimization Guide On Device Model → restart Chrome → delete the folder. Reshare so people know what's sitting on their computers.
>
> *Quoting @Pirat_Nation:* Google Chrome is quietly downloading a roughly 4 GB AI model to many users’ computers without clear upfront consent. The file, called weights.bin, is part of Google’s Gemini Nano on-device language model and lands in the browser’s user data folder under OptGuideOnDeviceModel. It powers built-in AI tools such as “Help me write,” smarter tab suggestions, on-device scam detection, and page summarization. The download triggers automatically for devices meeting minimum hardware requirements, and Chrome often replaces the files if deleted. While the model processes data locally, installation happens in the background with minimal notification. The scale is noteworthy. Hundreds of millions or billions of installations add up to thousands of tonnes of carbon emissions globally from data transfer, even though each is a one-time event. To prevent or remove it, go to chrome://flags, disable the entries for the optimization guide on-device model and Prompt API, restart the browser, and manually delete the folder.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/k1rallik/status/2051745051894522198
- **What:** Claims Chrome auto-installs a ~4GB Gemini Nano on-device model (weights.bin in OptGuideOnDeviceModel) and re-downloads it if deleted. Quoted Pirat_Nation post gives the neutral account (powers Help me write, scam detection); k1rallik adds alarmist scale/carbon framing and a chrome://flags opt-out.

> - FSA: ~$2,700+ in estimated savings

> You generally cannot double-dip.
>

>

## @intellectronica - A week of agentic Obsidian workflow notes
> A few notes on agentic @obsdmd (about a week in):
>
> - This is amazing. So fast, so flexible.
> - Bases for everything. All my notes have a `type` and matching template and structure. Bases organise them, the agent knows how to create, query, and update them.
> - All notes are top-level and linked by properties, tags, or links. Folders only for attachments, templates, etc...
> - Agent Client plugin (need to install from github using BRAT) is fantastic. I have a split window editor/agent at all times. I use it with @opencode ACP. Kudos to @rainbow_0219 🙏
> - @tobi's QMD is the perfect companion. I have it re-indexed regularly, the skill installed, and instructions for the agent to use it to search notes (remember to use `query` for hybrid semantic/keyword search).
> - The CLI is promising, but the fact that you can't run it (or sync or any of ther other functions) without having the GUI available is my biggest problem with Obsidian currently.
> - Vault syncing through Obsidian Sync for mobile access, but also via the Git plugin to GitHub, and via a cron job to my OpenClaw and OpenCode websservers. That means that I can easily work with the notes agentically, also without the Obsidian client UI.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/intellectronica/status/2025638214405697748
- **What:** Eleanor Berger's setup for agent-managed Obsidian: typed notes with templates organised via Bases, flat structure, Agent Client plugin with opencode ACP, tobi's QMD hybrid search, multi-path vault sync (Obsidian Sync, Git, cron to servers); main complaint is the Obsidian CLI needs the GUI running.

## @Legendaryy - Structured expert personas beat "you are an expert" prompts
> *Replying to @Legendaryy:* 1. EmotionPrompt (8-115% improvement) - Microsoft + Peking University tested adding emotional stakes to prompts, e.g. "this is very important to my career"; 8% gain on instruction tasks, 115% on complex reasoning; positive words account for 50-70% of improvement.

## @heynavtoor - AirLLM: 70B Models on a 4GB GPU via Layer-by-Layer Inference
> 🚨 BREAKING: Someone just made 70B parameter models run on a single 4GB GPU.
>
> It's called AirLLM. No quantization. No distillation. No pruning. Just raw 70B inference on hardware that costs less than a dinner.
>
> You can even run Llama 3.1 405B on 8GB VRAM.
>
> Here's how it works:
>
> → Decomposes the model layer-by-layer
> → Loads only one layer into GPU memory at a time
> → Runs inference, moves to the next layer
> → Prefetches the next layer while computing the current one
> → Supports 4-bit and 8-bit compression for 3x speed boost
>
> No cloud API. No $10K GPU. Just pip install airllm and go.
>
> It supports almost every major model — Llama, Qwen, Mistral, ChatGLM, Baichuan, InternLM — and it auto-detects the model type. Works on Linux, macOS (Apple Silicon), and Google Colab free tier. 100% Open Source. Apache 2.0 License.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/heynavtoor/status/2025181204505592213
- **What:** Promo thread for AirLLM, an open-source (Apache 2.0) library that runs 70B-405B models on 4-8GB GPUs by streaming one layer at a time into VRAM with prefetching, trading speed for memory; optional 4/8-bit compression gives ~3x speedup. Hype-heavy framing, so expect slow throughput.

## @chrysb - Five ways an OpenClaw agent shoots you in the foot: drift, trust, autonomy, cost, observability
> five ways openclaw agent will shoot you in foot. 1) drift: agent writes state everywhere (agents-md, memory-md, disk, databases); enforce where writes go, use git, review workspace nightly. 2) trust boundaries: untrusted input explodes attack surface; use separate sandboxed agents, code routes, AI reasons. 3) autonomy calibration: start read-only, graduate to filtered writes, earn full write. 4) cost discipline: cache stable ids, deterministic filtering, cheaper models for routine tasks. 5) observability: if you can't trace failure in five minutes it isn't production-ready; commit every change, rollback first-class. Treat agents like distributed systems, not chatbots.

- **Tweet:** https://x.com/chrysb/status/2023545992239608301
- **What:** Operational checklist for running OpenClaw agents in production: lock down where state is written, sandbox untrusted inputs, grant autonomy incrementally, cut LLM calls with deterministic code, and make failures traceable and rollbackable via git and logs.
